findings.ci_integration: The core repository added CI specifically to continuously test the released vision and dnn packages against Quidra changes before they land in develop/main, so core changes cannot silently break first-party packages, which is evidence of deliberate maintenance process rather than ad hoc releases.
findings.contributor_base: All observed pull requests across quidra-lang/quidra, quidra-lang/dnn, and quidra-lang/vision (core release PR, first-party package compatibility CI PR, and both packages' initial release PRs) are authored and merged by the same single account, koba-jon, who is also recorded as making dnn's and vision's first contributions.
findings.popularity_signals: quidra-lang/quidra, quidra-lang/dnn, and quidra-lang/vision each show 0 stars and 0 forks on their GitHub pages at snapshot time.
findings.recency: All release and PR activity observed (v0.1.0/v0.2.0 of core, dnn, and vision, plus the compatibility-CI and documentation-alignment PRs) occurred within a roughly 48-hour window on 2026-09-16 through 2026-09-18, i.e. very shortly before this evaluation's snapshot date, indicating the project is currently active but extremely young.
findings.release_cadence: Both dnn and vision have exactly two tagged releases each (v0.1.0 and v0.2.0), both cut within roughly 24-36 hours of each other on 2026-09-18, immediately following core Quidra's own v0.2.0 release. dnn v0.1.0 was released 18 Sep 04:53 and dnn v0.2.0 was released 18 Sep 16:25; vision v0.1.0 was released 18 Sep 04:53 and vision v0.2.0 was released 18 Sep 16:23.
findings.release_synchronization: Package releases are tied to core-language release order rather than independent cadence: the docs describe a fixed release order where each library updates its version and requires.quidra range and tests against the tagged core release only after a core release exists, and vision's v0.1.0 PR states it targets released Quidra v0.2.0 via requires.quidra = >=0.2.0 <0.3.0.

metric.package_ecosystem_activity_mainte.predeclared_target: The two known Quidra packages (quidra-lang/dnn, quidra-lang/vision) plus the core language repository (quidra-lang/quidra) were selected as the complete reachable universe per the domain-coverage sampling rule above; there is no larger population to sample from, so activity/maintenance evidence covers this full known universe rather than a probabilistic sample.
metric.package_ecosystem_activity_mainte.proxy_limitations: Star/fork counts are recorded as declared evidence per the methodology but are explicitly not used as a standalone proxy; they are near-zero for a project this new and are not comparable in scale to established ecosystems for other benchmarked languages.
metric.package_ecosystem_activity_mainte.retrieval_route: web_search against GitHub release/PR/repository pages, snapshot 2026-09-23.
metric.package_ecosystem_activity_mainte.score_rationale: Package ecosystem activity/maintenance is scored low (15/100). Positive signals exist (recent releases, an explicit cross-repository compatibility CI process, signed/verified release tags, structured versioning against core compatibility ranges), which keep the score above a floor of zero. However the entire observable ecosystem is two packages maintained by a single contributor inside the language's own organization, with zero external stars/forks/independent contributors and only two releases each in a ~48-hour window, so there is essentially no independent community maintenance signal yet. This reflects genuine, verified sparseness rather than missing evidence, so it is scored low rather than marked N/A.

findings.dnn_description: dnn is Quidra's first-party deep-neural-network package. It provides layers, activations, losses, and optimizers as ordinary Quidra source code on top of the standard tensor and neural foundations.
findings.dnn_domain: quidra-lang/dnn covers the machine-learning/DNN domain only.
findings.domains_with_zero_coverage: No library (first-party or third-party) was found via targeted search for: web/HTTP framework, database/ORM, testing framework beyond built-in, serialization beyond built-in JSON, CLI framework beyond built-in, logging, date/time extension, or cryptography/security. 8 of the 10 declared domains returned no evidence of any library.
findings.known_packages: Web search located exactly two published Quidra source packages, both under the quidra-lang GitHub organization (the same organization that maintains the compiler itself), not independent third-party authors: quidra-lang/dnn and quidra-lang/vision.
findings.no_awesome_list_or_broader_index: No community-curated list (e.g. an 'awesome-quidra' list) or any additional non-org package repository was found by web search.
findings.registry_existence: Quidra has no central third-party package registry/index (no npm/crates.io/PyPI equivalent). The docs/packages.md file embedded in this packet confirms package resolution is Git-based: a bare 'quidra-dnn' name resolves to https://github.com/quidra-lang/dnn.git, and third-party packages use 'owner/repository' or an explicit Git URL, but no discovery index exists for enumerating them.
findings.third_party_independence_caveat: Both discovered packages are maintained inside the same GitHub organization (quidra-lang) that owns the compiler and are described in the language's own docs as 'first-party' rather than independently authored third-party contributions, so even the 2/10 domain coverage found is not evidence of an independent third-party ecosystem.
findings.vision_description: vision is Quidra's first-party tensor image-processing package.
findings.vision_domain: quidra-lang/vision covers the image/computer-vision domain only.

predeclared_sampling.candidate_universe: Fixed checklist of 10 language-neutral library domains evaluated identically for every language in this benchmark run: (1) Web/HTTP server or client framework beyond a bare built-in, (2) Database driver/ORM, (3) Testing framework beyond the language's own built-in assert facility, (4) Serialization beyond built-in JSON, (5) CLI argument-parsing framework beyond a built-in facility, (6) Logging framework, (7) Image/computer-vision processing, (8) Machine learning / deep learning (DNN), (9) Date/time extension beyond built-in, (10) Cryptography/security library.
predeclared_sampling.retrieval_route: Provider-brokered web_search tool against public GitHub pages (github.com/quidra-lang/*, release/PR pages) and general web queries; no authenticated GitHub API access was available.
predeclared_sampling.selection_rule: For Quidra, because no third-party package registry/index exists, the frozen selection rule is: (a) read the language's own docs/packages.md for the canonical package-resolution convention (unquoted bare name -> quidra-lang/<name>, or explicit owner/repository Git URL) and any named example packages; (b) enumerate every repository under the quidra-lang GitHub organization via web search; (c) for each of the 10 declared domains, run one targeted web search for 'quidra' + domain keyword to look for any independently published (non quidra-lang-org) library. This rule and the domain list were fixed before evidence collection and applied uniformly; the same retrieval route (web_search, GitHub project pages) and depth (one targeted query per domain plus org enumeration) is intended to be used for every language in this benchmark.

metric.third_party_library_availability_.proxy_limitations: GitHub star/fork counts were observed (0 stars, 0 forks on all three quidra-lang repositories checked) but are not used as the scoring basis by themselves; they are recorded only as corroborating context per the methodology's restriction on raw popularity proxies.
metric.third_party_library_availability_.score_rationale: Domain coverage is scored low (10/100) because only 2 of the 10 predeclared common library domains have any published library at all, and both of those are first-party/organization-maintained rather than an independently emerging third-party ecosystem. This is a rubric-defined low score for a genuinely and verifiably sparse ecosystem, not an N/A: the metric intentionally tests for library availability and a near-total absence of coverage is itself the finding.
